entries.notes: Kind convention, so there is no refutation field. The finding's scaling example is read as the refutation. TeX (l.425): nu_train is a training probability distribution on S, with lambda << nu_train, ||d lambda/d nu_train||_inf < infinity and b > 0. Algorithm 1 takes b >= 1 + ||d lambda/d nu_train||_inf, 'for which the loss controls the sampling error'. Lean: EGF.loss_controls_sampling_essSup takes nu_train to be any sigma-finite Measure S (a probability is one). It assumes hnuT : lam << nutrain, hM : essSup (lam.rnDeriv nutrain) nutrain != infinity, hb : 1 + essSup.toReal <= b and a finite loss. The penalty is b * integral of delta f_init against nu_train. With nu_train a probability, the paper's E_{s ~ nu_train} (v2 l.163: the law nu/nu(S)) is Lean's integral. So Eq. (15) is klwfmLoss at the same nu_train and b, and the threshold is exactly hb. The remaining Lean hypotheses belong to earlier entries and are unchanged here: F_init and kappa probabilities, F_init and F_out << lambda, InflowAC (from the nonsingular moves, C-6), kappa << lambda, finite entropy (l.494) and a finite loss. The text's 'the loss controls the sampling error' is weaker than the Lean conclusion, which gives H(kappa) <= L and TV <= (1/sqrt 2) sqrt(L - H) + min(1, N (L - H)). loss_controls_defect holds likewise, with N the essSup (lambda <= N nu_train, le_essSup_rnDeriv_smul). added_hypotheses ('nu_train a probability measure on S') is in the text as 'training probability distribution nu_train on S'. Nothing else was added: '(a law of the states of training paths, as in Algorithm 1)' is a gloss, and it is consistent with Algorithm 1's p_t-weighted law. The scaling example is no longer covered. On Bool with counting lambda, nu_train = 5 lambda has mass 10 and is not a probability. Its normalization lambda/2 gives the threshold 1 + 2 = 3, as the finding says, so b = 1.2 is excluded. The other uses of nu_train are consistent: l.204 (the FM loss, scale-free under l.163's convention), l.395 (the uniform distribution on the vertices, a probability), l.429 and l.482.

Kind gap, added_hypotheses [], and none was added. 'B trajectories in each of B-> and B<-' describes the algorithm as run, and m >= 1 is derived. (1) At l.457, |B| = 2B, which matches the display's 1/(2B). (2) At l.465, the dispatch's question: is nu_train normalized by m? Let nu(A) = E[(1/2B) sum_{s in B} sum_{t <= t_max} p_t(s) 1_A(s_t)]. Then nu(S) = m. 'The p_t-weighted law of the states of the buffer's paths' is a law: a probability by C-64, and for an unnormalized measure the paper's convention (v2 l.163) is nu/nu(S). So nu_train = nu/m, and the m the text defines is exactly that normalizer. The text never writes nu_train = nu/m, but that is the natural reading and the only one under which the sentence holds. The self-normalized E[nu-hat/nu-hat(S)] would not give the exact identity. By linearity, the display's expectation is b * integral of delta f_init against nu, minus E_kappa log f-hat_term, which equals (b m) E_{nu_train} delta f_init - E_kappa log f-hat_term. That is Eq. (15) at weight b m, so 'a Monte-Carlo estimate of (15) with b replaced by b m' is exact. It is a definitional identity. Loss.lean's SCOPE says the estimator is not formalized, and it needs nothing beyond linearity of expectation. Why m >= 1: p_1 = 1 is the empty product, and every p_t >= 0 because each factor lies in (0,1] (l.474-476, C-3 and C-38), so each of the 2B paths contributes at least 1. Also m <= t_max. The threshold holds: b m >= b >= 1 + ||d lambda/d nu_train||_inf (m >= 1, b > 0). EGF.loss_controls_sampling_essSup holds at every weight above the threshold, here at b m, with its bound in terms of L_{bm} - H(kappa). Faithful, no overclaim. With |B| = B the mean weight would be only >= 1/2, which is the gap the first edit closes. Wording: '(so that b m >= b)' states the consequence of m >= 1. What is used is b m >= b >= 1 + ||...||_inf, i.e. the weight of the estimated loss meets the threshold. It reads correctly as written, and the marker says so (optional wording in finding 1). nu_train and m depend on the current parameters, as C-59's on-policy nu_train already did, and the control holds at each theta. Layout: see finding 1.

Kind gap. Mathlib's aeconst_of_dense_aestabilizer_smul needs the following. G is a group with a topology and a continuous inverse. X is an R1 Borel space. mu is finite and inner regular. G acts continuously (ContinuousSMul), and ErgodicSMul G X mu holds (it includes SMulInvariantMeasure: mu is preserved). s is null-measurable and its ae-stabilizer is dense. Then s is null or conull. EGF.ae_const_of_dense_rotations applies it with G = SO(n), X = S^{n-1} and mu = sphereVolume n, through EGF.ergodicSMul_rotSphere (n >= 2). The subgroup generated by the Phi_i lies in the ae-stabilizer. The TeX setting is 'a finite Borel measure on a compact metric space preserved by the action ... a group acting continuously and ergodically'. It implies every side condition. A metric space is T2, hence R1. 'Borel' is BorelSpace. Inner regularity is automatic, which answers the dispatch's question with yes: Mathlib's instance instInnerRegularOfIsCompletelyPseudoMetrizableSpace makes every finite Borel measure on a second-countable completely metrizable space inner regular, and a compact metric space is both. 'Preserved' and 'ergodically' together are ErgodicSMul. Continuous inversion is not needed for a dense subgroup. H = H^{-1}, so H lies in {g : (g .)^{-1}(s) =ae s}, and Mathlib's aeconst_of_dense_setOf_preimage_smul_ae (no ContinuousInv) applies. SO_{d+1}(R) is a topological group anyway. lambda on S^d (sphereVolume: finite, rotation invariant) is an instance of the setting, as the text says. The paragraph's conclusion is unchanged: density gives ergodicity on S^d, d >= 1 (isGroupErgodic_sphereRotGroup_of_dense, hn : 2 <= n). The entry's added_hypotheses (the step's setting) is in the text verbatim, and nothing else was added. The finding's counterexample (R with counting measure and the dense subgroup Q) is excluded twice: counting measure on R is not finite, and R is not compact.

Kind gap, added_hypotheses []. Sentence by sentence. 'A a measurable set with lambda(h^{-1}(A) symdiff A) = 0' gives 1_A o h = 1_A a.e. That is the hypothesis hinv of EGF.norm_mFourierCoeff_eq_of_invariant (|f^(A^T k)| = |f^(k)|). Its hA : IsUnit det is implied by h being in Aff(T^d), whose linear parts lie in SL_d(Z) (v2 l.318). '1_A is a.e. constant, and h is ergodic' is EGF.ergodic_of_mFourierCoeff. Its criterion quantifies over f with f o T =ae f, i.e. over almost invariant sets. The text concludes the a.e. form (every almost invariant set of h is null or conull), which for a measure-preserving h is Mathlib's Ergodic. 'A set almost invariant under the Phi_i is almost invariant under every element of the group, the moves preserving lambda' is EGF.ae_invariant_of_mem_closure: the generators and their inverses are measure-preserving, because affine maps of T^d with unimodular linear part preserve Haar measure. That is the setting, and 'the moves preserving lambda' names it. 'An ergodic map has no almost invariant set other than null and conull ones' is QuasiErgodic.ae_empty_or_univ0, as used in EGF.isGroupErgodic_of_ergodic_mem. 'One ergodic element makes the group ergodic' is that theorem. Its IsGroupErgodic quantifies over the group, and Definition 3.1's form (over the generators, DEC-146) follows through ae_invariant_of_mem_closure, which the new sentence states. Faithful. No added hypothesis: lambda being preserved is the setting, not a new assumption. C-28's sentence at l.909 ('a set A invariant under the group would give the invariant mean-zero function 1_A - lambda(A)') stays, as the entry rules. In L^2, invariance is a.e., and the passage from the generators to the group that it relies on is now stated at l.915.

Kind gap, added_hypotheses []. The edited sentence reads: 'Ergodicity guarantees, for a model rich enough (Theorems 3.4, 3.5 and 3.6), that the parameterized family is universal: for any probability distributions F_init, F_term << lambda with bounded density it contains flows from F_init to F_term with arbitrarily small errors ..., even with ... affine maps on tori and rotations on spheres.' Every reading of it is within the Lean. A family of generative flows (any family) containing a policy ergodic for a finite invariant lambda-hat ~ lambda, with paired outflows dense in the non-negative cone, is epsilon-universal: EGF.universality_of_ergodic_family. Tori: EGF.universality_tori_of_ergodic (group ergodic, rich model). Spheres: EGF.universality_sphere (density) and EGF.universality_sphere_of_ergodic (group ergodicity alone). So 'ergodicity guarantees' holds for rotations too, more generally than Theorem 3.6's density. 'Universal' is Definition 3.2's epsilon form (DEC-141), which the colon clause restates. Dropping 'of EGFs' removes the implicit claim that the affine toroidal and isometry spherical families are families of EGFs. Since C-54 they are EGFs only where the group of the moves is ergodic (AffineToroidalModel.isEGFErgodic_flow_iff, isEGFErgodic_sphere_iff). The references render 'Theorems 3.4, 3.5 and 3.6'. Pointing to Theorem 3.4, which still says 'family of EGF', is not an overclaim: the sentence claims no more than the Lean. That hypothesis is OQ-106 (b) (finding 2). The marker attributes the replaced '(Theorem 3.4) ... family of EGFs' to C-18's text, and C-18's commit a1ddcb0 introduced it.

Kind typo, no anchor: 0-flows are not formalized. With F_init = F_term = 0, constraint (2), F_init + F_out pi* = F_term + F_out, reads xi pi* = xi. In Lean, EGF.IsFlowMatching pi xi 0 0 is Finit + inflow pi xi = Fterm + xi. So 'the outflows of the generative flows (pi*, xi) satisfying (2) with F_init = F_term = 0' are exactly the invariant measures of the first clause. The gloss now carries the constraint that the bare 'generative flows' lacked, a generative flow being any pair (v2 l.165). The pair is written policy first, as at v2 l.165 and in EGF.GenerativeFlow. The constraint reference renders as '(2)'. A generative flow's outflow is finite (l.165), so the gloss reads 'measures' as finite measures, as Section 2 does throughout. The introduction's gloss (l.142, C-51) has the same first clause and is consistent. added_hypotheses [].

Kind missing-hypothesis, added_hypotheses []. First clause: 'Theorems 3.5 and 3.6 ask of the moves only that the group they generate be ergodic, respectively dense'. Of the moves, Theorem 3.5 asks only that the generated group be ergodic (universality_tori_of_ergodic, herg); membership in Aff(T^d) is part of the family's definition. Theorem 3.6 asks only density in SO_{d+1}(R) (universality_sphere, hdense). The rich model both theorems also ask for is a condition on the model, not on the moves. So 'of the moves only' is exact where the old 'only' was loose (C-31's richness; EGF.not_isUniversalFamilyEps_sphere_of_constantHeads shows it is needed). Second clause: 'so the two inverse moves among the four of Section 3.1 are not needed'. Two moves generate the same group as the two moves with their inverses, so the hypotheses hold with p = 2. Anchors: EGF.universality_tori_two_moves (S and T on T^2, every translation, rich model, members EGFs) and, on S^2, FamiliesOfRecord's so3Pair_dense and universality_sphere_two_moves_three. 'The four' are 'the two generators and their inverses' of l.333 and l.354. The reference renders 'Section 3.1'. C-56's single-move clause (exists_universality_tori_single_move) is unchanged. The new wording also removes the reading 'the inverse of each of the four moves'.

findings.what: These are the corrector's points on Theorem 3.4 and l.512. Both are real as wording, neither is false, and neither was created by this batch. (a) Theorem 3.4 (l.310, v1 l.277) reads 'A parameterized family of EGF is universal provided ...'. 'Of EGF' is a hypothesis the Lean does not need: EGF.universality_of_ergodic_family holds for any family of generative flows, which is Lean >= paper. The theorem as printed stays true. Dropping the hypothesis strengthens a true theorem, so it is the author's call: OQ-106 (b), still OPEN. C-68's pointer to it is not an overclaim. (b) l.512 (v1 l.432, outside every entry's printed sites) reads 'An EGF family is built by randomly choosing diffeomorphisms from affine toroidal families on T^2 and from isometry spherical families on S^2'. It uses the same 'family of EGF' wording. Read as a description of the experiments, it holds. On T^2 the moves include S^{+-1}, T^{+-1} (C-34's harness), so the generated group is ergodic at every translation: EGF.isGroupErgodic_minimalMoves, and a larger group stays ergodic. On S^2, randomly chosen rotations generate a dense subgroup almost surely, but nothing in Lean says so. C-68 does not make l.512 inconsistent, because it changed only the Expressivity sentence.
